title: Counter
statement:
Write `createCounter(n)`, which takes an integer `n` and returns a function `counter` that takes no arguments. The first call of `counter` gives back `n`, and every later call gives back one more than the call before it: `n`, `n + 1`, `n + 2`, and so on.

Each case gives `n` and a list `calls` in which every entry is `"call"`, meaning `counter()` is invoked once. The answer is the list of values those invocations return, in order.
notes:
## Intuition

The returned function has to remember something between calls: how far it has counted. A local variable inside `counter` would be created afresh on every call, so the state has to live one level out, in `createCounter`. Because `counter` is defined inside `createCounter`, it keeps access to that variable even after `createCounter` has returned. That pairing of a function with the variables around it is a **closure**. (The brute force keeps a list of every value handed out and derives the next one from its length; it works but stores far more than it needs.)

## Approach

1. In `createCounter`, store the next value to hand out in `count`, starting at `n`.
2. Return a function that reads the current `count` into `value`,
3. adds 1 to `count` for the next call,
4. and returns `value`.

## Example 1, step by step

With `n = 10`, `count` starts at 10.

- First call: `value = 10`, `count` becomes 11, 10 is returned.
- Second call: `value = 11`, `count` becomes 12, 11 is returned.
- Third call: `value = 12`, `count` becomes 13, 12 is returned.

The answer is `[10, 11, 12]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) per call: one read, one addition.
- Space: O(1): a single number lives in the closure.

## Pitfalls

- Incrementing before reading returns `n + 1` on the first call. In the one-line form `return count++;` the postfix `++` is what makes it right; `++count` is off by one.
- Declaring `count` inside the inner function resets it on every call, so every call returns `n`.
- Two counters made by separate `createCounter` calls must not share state; a variable outside `createCounter` would make them interfere.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `n` | the first value the counter returns |
| `count` | the value the next call will return, kept in the closure |
| `value` | the number this call returns |

narration.1: createCounter runs once and sets up the state the counter will share.
narration.2: count holds the next value to hand out; it starts at n and outlives this call.
narration.3: Return the counter itself, a function that closes over count.
narration.4: Each call first reads the value it will return.
narration.5: Advance count so the following call returns one more.
narration.6: Hand back the value read before the increment.
